access_time_note: Web calls do not provide a per-page UTC timestamp; this conservative interval brackets the source-review session. No access time was invented at individual-page precision.
source_id_policy: Stable source IDs for this stage; IDs are not silently rebound.
method: Independent discovery used the released hypothetical brief plus public primary sources only. No case-specific field observation, site record, installation file, rainfall series, model, test, or repair was available or executed.

sources.title: Bioretention Design Handbook: Designing Holistic Bioretention for Performance and Longevity
sources.locator: Ch. 4 §4.1, drainage area delineation (handbook pp. 4-2–4-3); Ch. 6 §§6.3–6.6, inlet types, placement, sizing and flow-path modifications (pp. 6-7–6-28); Ch. 7 §§7.1–7.3, pretreatment; Ch. 13 §§13.1–13.3, construction and inspection; Ch. 14 §14.2, maintenance. Text rendering locators are also recorded in the local sources index.
sources.observed_operation: Opened EPA's official NEPIS text rendering and inspected the listed handbook sections; also used official EPA listing for release number/date. No code, model, field test, or design calculation was run.
sources.governing_conditions_defaults_exceptions: Capture depends on catchment boundary, grade, alignment and orientation of the inlet, inlet opening and debris, number/placement of inlets, and rainfall flow. Offline configurations may accept a controlled portion and bypass excess down-gutter; online configurations receive runoff into the facility and require a safe overflow path. Pretreatment can localize debris/sediment and dissipate energy, but introduces maintenance needs. Underdrain/outlet behavior is a separate path. Examples are conditional on local geometry, design intent, safety, maintenance capacity, and local standards.
sources.applicability_and_limits: Useful for a qualified partner to screen mechanisms and alternatives only. The case has no surveyed drainage boundary, elevations, inlet/overflow drawings, or known jurisdiction. Do not transfer handbook sizes, thresholds, details, or reported performance into a construction design.
sources.issue_fix_regression_release_history: Static 2023 release. Ch. 6 recounts NYC replacing some first-generation inlets with depressed curb cuts or modified back-plates after conveyance problems, and Portland adding bars after vehicles could enter an opening; these are historical issue/fix examples with different local geometry and safety tradeoffs, not a proposed site repair. No later handbook revision or errata was established in the accessed source.

sources.title: Rain gardens (bioretention) 101
sources.publisher: Minnesota Pollution Control Agency, Minnesota Stormwater Manual
sources.released_version_or_commit: Living online manual page; no page revision, release number, or commit was displayed in the accessed page.
sources.locator: Sections “How does a rain garden work?”, “Why would I need an underdrain?”, and “What maintenance is needed?”; accessed rendering lines 62–91.
sources.observed_operation: Opened and read the official MPCA page sections; no site assessment or local-standard determination was performed.
sources.governing_conditions_defaults_exceptions: The page distinguishes no-underdrain gardens, where captured water can infiltrate into underlying soil, from underdrained gardens, where captured water can be conveyed to a sewer. It describes curb cuts as one routing method, ponding followed by percolation or underdrain flow, typical drainage in a day or two, and routine inspection of entry points for clogging. These are general descriptions, not universal limits.
sources.applicability_and_limits: Supports separate capture, temporary storage, and drawdown questions. Minnesota guidance is an example only because the site jurisdiction and the garden's actual underdrain/media are unknown. Do not treat its generic timing as a project-specific compliance finding.
sources.issue_fix_regression_release_history: No dated page revision or issue/fix history was visible in the accessed live page.

sources.title: Operation and maintenance of bioretention and other stormwater infiltration practices
sources.publisher: Minnesota Pollution Control Agency, Minnesota Stormwater Manual
sources.released_version_or_commit: Living online manual page; no page revision, release number, or commit was displayed in the accessed page.
sources.locator: Post-construction phase O&M and troubleshooting table; accessed rendering lines 156–212, particularly 170–205.
sources.observed_operation: Opened and read the official MPCA page; no maintenance was carried out.
sources.governing_conditions_defaults_exceptions: The general table suggests first-year post-storm checks after events over 0.5 inches, then checks including 48 hours after rain and when ground is not frozen; the page notes deep sumps may retain water. Troubleshooting associates prolonged standing water with possible fine-sediment surface clogging, ineffective pretreatment, or high sediment loading; absence of flow may reflect leaves, sediment, trash, or plant debris; inlet scour may relate to obstruction or improper grading. It also says mulch can clog inlets/outlets/bypass pipes. These are possible causes and contextual schedules, not a unique diagnosis or universal requirement.
sources.applicability_and_limits: Directly informs what to inspect and log given the stated recent leaf clearing and mulch addition. Applicability depends on actual design and local rules; do not prescribe scraping, aeration, vacuuming, or another repair from this research alone.
sources.issue_fix_regression_release_history: No dated page revision or issue/fix history was visible in the accessed live page.

sources.title: Alleviating compaction from construction activities
sources.publisher: Minnesota Pollution Control Agency, Minnesota Stormwater Manual
sources.released_version_or_commit: Living online manual page; the page displays no current revision identifier. A linked MPCA PDF search result shows a 2021-06-15 document date, but this review relied on the live page.
sources.locator: Causes/effects, identifying compaction, effectiveness of methods, and applicability sections; accessed rendering lines 103–106, 222–244 and 267 onward.
sources.observed_operation: Opened and read the official MPCA page; no soil measurement or infiltration test was performed.
sources.governing_conditions_defaults_exceptions: The page describes compaction from equipment, storage, excavation and traffic; wet and clay soils as more susceptible; and reduced porosity/permeability as mechanisms. Ponding, weak plant growth and erosion may be clues, but it distinguishes observations from soil measurements. It states restoration must be tailored to site conditions and discourages prescriptive restoration specifications. It notes measurement-method limitations and reports mixed evidence on tillage versus amendments.
sources.applicability_and_limits: Makes the delivery a plausible lead only; it does not show that compaction occurred at this hypothetical site. Surface ponding alone is not diagnostic. Any future soil characterization or remediation belongs to a qualified partner after permission and after installation/media/underdrain records are reviewed.
sources.issue_fix_regression_release_history: The page references multiple prior studies and says compaction alleviation remains an active research area; reported intervention results vary. No live-page revision history was displayed. This is a reason not to claim one universal fix.

sources.title: Green Infrastructure Installation, Operation, and Maintenance
sources.released_version_or_commit: Current EPA web guidance as accessed; no fixed release number or revision date was visible in the page.
sources.locator: Construction, operation and maintenance, municipal plans, and inspection/maintenance tracking; accessed rendering lines 4–64.
sources.observed_operation: Opened and read the official EPA page; no inspection or maintenance was carried out.
sources.governing_conditions_defaults_exceptions: EPA says installation tasks depend on the green-infrastructure type; avoid compaction or clogging during construction, maintain written plans and schedules, identify responsible parties, and track maintenance/inspection. Heavy equipment is discouraged for routine maintenance because it can compact soil or damage roots. Local codes determine actual owner obligations.
sources.applicability_and_limits: Supports requesting installation/maintenance documents and separating owner routines from repairs. It is national program guidance, not a binding local standard for an unidentified city or this hypothetical garden.
sources.issue_fix_regression_release_history: No fixed edition/revision history was shown in the accessed page.

sources.title: Assessing the performance of stormwater Best Management Practices (BMPs)
sources.publisher: Minnesota Pollution Control Agency, Minnesota Stormwater Manual
sources.released_version_or_commit: Living manual page. It identifies an assessment manual developed in 2010 and notes a related Stormwater BMP Inspection and Maintenance Resource Guide update issued June 2024.
sources.locator: Four levels of assessment and summary table; accessed rendering lines 59–85.
sources.observed_operation: Opened and read the official MPCA page and its assessment-level summary; no assessment level was executed at the site.
sources.governing_conditions_defaults_exceptions: Level 1 visual inspection is described as quick and inexpensive but limited; capacity testing and simulated runoff provide different information and can have substantial effort/uncertainty or limited scope; Level 4 monitoring is most comprehensive but the page lists high effort and a typical 14-month elapsed time. The page says owners seeking credit from testing should consult the MPCA or another regulator.
sources.applicability_and_limits: Supports a modest observation-first proposal and a clear boundary between visual diagnosis and quantitative performance claims. The numerical effort/timing are generic manual estimates, not a schedule commitment or result for this site.
sources.issue_fix_regression_release_history: The page records a 2010 assessment manual and a June 2024 related-guide update; the current live manual page itself has no displayed commit/version.

sources.title: Water balance monitoring for two bioretention gardens in Omaha, Nebraska, 2011–14
sources.released_version_or_commit: USGS Scientific Investigations Report 2015–5188; first posted 2016-01-29; DOI 10.3133/sir20155188.
sources.locator: Abstract; report section “Water Balance Monitoring”, “Performance on an Event Basis”, including event examples in report text.
sources.observed_operation: Read USGS publication metadata/abstract and report text; did not download or reanalyze the monitoring data.
sources.governing_conditions_defaults_exceptions: The study measured inflow and outflow at two Omaha gardens. At one garden, results varied by event size; the report discusses rainfall amount, maximum intensity, duration and antecedent dry period. It gives two roughly similar-depth events with different durations/intensities and different outflow. Events with ponding above the report's 0.7-ft analysis limit were excluded from event analyses, and a second site had no recorded overflow.
sources.applicability_and_limits: Supports logging storm depth, duration/intensity, antecedent conditions, inflow and overflow separately. It is a study of two designed, instrumented gardens in Omaha; neither the event results nor numerical performance can be transferred to this unmeasured site. Covariates changed together, so a single-event comparison cannot isolate a cause.
sources.issue_fix_regression_release_history: Static numbered-series report, issued January 2016; no later correction/version history was identified in the accessed publication record.

sources.title: Evaluation of turf-grass and prairie-vegetated rain gardens in a clay and sand soil, Madison, Wisconsin, water years 2004–08
sources.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey with University of Wisconsin coauthor
sources.released_version_or_commit: USGS Scientific Investigations Report 2010–5077; first posted 2010-06-11.
sources.locator: Publication abstract and report text describing the five-year event record and comparisons of clay/sand and turf/prairie sites.
sources.observed_operation: Read USGS publication record and abstract; no underlying data were reanalyzed.
sources.governing_conditions_defaults_exceptions: Two purpose-built, roof-fed gardens with different soils and vegetation were monitored. The abstract states precipitation intensity and antecedent dry days influenced when underlying storage became saturated; reported performance also differed by soil and vegetation. The study uses a defined contributing-area ratio and design that are not known here.
sources.applicability_and_limits: Supports considering antecedent conditions, soil, vegetation and temporary storage separately. Results apply to those Madison sites and water years only; they do not establish the soil, drainage, or capacity of this curb-fed hypothetical garden.
sources.issue_fix_regression_release_history: Static numbered-series report, posted in 2010; no later correction/version history was identified in the accessed publication record.

sources.title: Evaluating Green Infrastructure Stormwater Capture Performance under Extreme Precipitation
sources.publisher: Journal of Extreme Events; author record hosted by Drexel University; World Scientific Publishing
sources.released_version_or_commit: Journal of Extreme Events, volume 3 issue 2, article 1650006; June 2016; DOI 10.1142/S2345737616500068.
sources.locator: Drexel-hosted article record and abstract, especially study setting and findings (record lines 5–29).
sources.observed_operation: Read the university-hosted article metadata and abstract; full article details beyond that record were not asserted.
sources.governing_conditions_defaults_exceptions: The abstract describes a Queens, New York facility monitored during 2011–2014, with sandy native soils and a low 3.8:1 hydraulic loading ratio. It reports that inlet bypass often limited capture despite high infiltration and that event duration, total precipitation and peak hourly intensity were associated with capture performance; maintenance frequency was described as a possible, anecdotal factor.
sources.applicability_and_limits: Direct evidence that capture failure can be distinct from slow infiltration. Its setting and site-specific ratios and percentages are not predictive for this case; maintenance causality was not established.
sources.issue_fix_regression_release_history: Static 2016 journal article/issue. The abstract states future work would examine other drivers of inlet bypass, including maintenance frequency; this is unresolved research, not a proven fix. No correction history was identified in the accessed author record.

sources.title: Overview for bioretention
sources.publisher: Minnesota Pollution Control Agency, Minnesota Stormwater Manual
sources.released_version_or_commit: Living online manual page; no page revision, release number, or commit was displayed in the accessed page.
sources.locator: Water quantity treatment section, high-flow bypass types; accessed rendering lines 110–123.
sources.observed_operation: Opened the official MPCA page through the indexed page result and read the water-quantity/bypass section; no design calculation was performed.
sources.governing_conditions_defaults_exceptions: The page describes bypass when a cell reaches its maximum ponding depth; it prefers offline designs where feasible to reduce internal erosion, and describes online overflow options. If offline design is not achievable, it emphasizes short flow paths for high flows and energy dissipation. Actual configuration depends on site and local criteria.
sources.applicability_and_limits: Useful for naming distinct routing alternatives and safe downstream questions; not a proposal to alter the curb or specify an overflow for this site.
sources.issue_fix_regression_release_history: The page links a June 2022 PDF snapshot, but no current live-page revision/commit was displayed. No site-specific problem history is available.
